An extraordinary second encounter—comparable only to the first, on 30 January 1955, with the story of Stephen in Acts of the Apostles, chapter 7, concerning the killing of the heir by the Jews.
It happened during High Mass, at home in my study, among the books that fell into my hands at precisely this hour while I was staying away from Mass.
Here all the oracles of vibration resonate together.
So this was the second encounter of this kind.
And it makes me certain that Hegel’s Phenomenology of Spirit is an inspired book of the German faith.

“It seems to it—to self-consciousness that has become reason—when it grasps itself in this way, namely by recognizing that its thought is immediately reality itself, as though the world had only now come into existence for it.

Before this, it does not understand the world. It desires it and works upon it; it withdraws from it and destroys it for itself, and destroys itself as consciousness: both as consciousness of the world as essential being and as consciousness of its nothingness.
Only now, after the grave has lost its truth, after the destruction of its reality has itself been destroyed … does it discover –––– its new real
So: first the grave must be lost.
That means the dead God must have risen again.
Therefore this begins with the end of the Crusades, just as Kojève correctly says (Introduction, p. 81).
That is what I read today in Kojève, during the Corpus Christi procession of 1955.
Here, to lose the grave means resurrection: the destruction of destruction, the killing of death.
Several thousand Göttingen Sevens have appeared in Göttingen and gloriously defeated one poor devil.

The relationship to 1837 is clear. These new fairy-tale brothers of 1955 stand in relation to their model of 1837 exactly as their opponent, poor Schlüter, stands in relation to the opponent of 1837, King Ernst August of Hanover. What a happy age, in which seven thousand Göttingen Sevens can suddenly be found!

I formulated my opinion on the Schlüter case in Göttingen, June 1955, for Johannes Gross, though in the end I did not send him all of it. University professors and students forced Schlüter to resign as minister of education through public demonstrations because he had published writings by university teachers who had been removed from their posts. The whole demonstration against him succeeded because it was directed from left against right and could exploit serious defects in Schlüter’s own character. So my opinion:
The whole thing: a guaranteed, risk-free way of satisfying the enormous pent-up demand for displays of civil courage!

Its constitutional significance: a minister brought down through action outside parliament; a recall. A test case for mobilizing the plebiscitary elements that cannot be eradicated from any democracy, but which after 1945—especially in the Bonn Basic Law and in the debate over rearmament—were carefully and anxiously suppressed.

Its historical importance: the numerous Göttingen Sevens of 1955 stand in relation to the originals of 1837 exactly as their opponent in 1955, poor Herr Schlüter, stands in relation to the opponent of 1837, King Ernst August of Hanover.
That is a clear and exact measure of their respective historical rank.
The aesthetic quality of the event:

University professors and students, with political permission, manfully throw themselves upon one poor unlucky fool in order to cure him thoroughly of his delusion of grandeur—the idea that he might become the minister responsible for universities.
As a spectacle, this is more a nightmare in the manner of Kafka than a drama of freedom in the manner of William Tell.
the wild-boar thief as overthrower of ministers.
(The whole thing: a guaranteed, risk-free way of satisfying society’s accumulated demand for displays of civil courage.)
Magnus homo / magno homini: magnus homo. Great man to great man: great man.
Magnus homo / parvo homini: Deus. Great man to small man: God.
Parvus homo / parvo homini: Homo. Small man to small man: man.
But where has the wolf gone?! I think the closest answer is this: wherever homo homini homo—man is man to man, whether great or small—means equality, man is closer to the wolf than to God.
Magnus homo / parvus Deus et magnus lupus.
The great man: a little God and a great wolf.

Progress upon progress: the Göttingen Seven of 1837 have become the Göttingen Three Thousand of 1955! In the July issue of Der Monat, an essay actually describes them under precisely this title: “The Göttingen Three Thousand.” The unconscious accuracy of a hack.
But why not simply call them seven thousand? Or at least three thousand five hundred? Four-thousandfold resistance to authority. What an enormous success for re-education!

And behold: there is also a Mensch-Nahme—a taking of man! A man takes a woman, and she knows him. The slave hunter does not “take” the slave. He robs and sells him, just as the hunter takes wild game. But Hegel’s taking of God is at the same time a taking of man by the God-taker.
Hic Rhodus! Hic saltat! Hinc illae lacrimae!
Here is Rhodes! Jump here! Hence those tears!
So the only thing left, following Heidegger’s example, is to write in future: Being, crossed out. Man, crucified.

A happy encounter with a remark by James-Hamlet: when the jurist Sir Edward Coke told the king that he was “defended by the laws,” the king replied that this was “foolish.” A king, he said, is not protected by laws but by God. Is that not magnificent?
And place it as the polar—or dialectical—opposite of Rivarol: L’obscurité protège mieux que la loi. Obscurity protects better than the law.

Immeasurable happiness in discoveries and encounters like these. And who gave me this encounter with James-Hamlet’s remark? Isaac Disraeli—the father of the famous Disraeli, Lord Beaconsfield—in his Character of James the First, p. 423 (Works of I. D., London 1859, <…>).
It is enough to make one Disraelitic!
“Protection exists only outside contemporary history. L’obscurité protège mieux. Obscurity protects better.”
A Gessler’s hat falls from its pole.
A cloud of fading printer’s ink and radio sound-gas settles over both worlds—East and West, servitude and freedom.
Apparently this industrious master-exploiter, in relation to both worlds, was the higher third term: the fulfillment of their ideal of intellectually elevated comfort.
Now, to begin with, the memory of this product sweated out by the culture industry will itself become a Gessler’s hat.
But as I write the words “Gessler’s hat,” I realize how comfortably old-fashioned and harmless my language still is.
Today the world resembles a totem clan with taboos more than it resembles a medieval Swiss peasant tribe with an imperial governor named Gessler and a William Tell.
When I think back to the years 1928–32, and when Adolf Caspary, Leo Strauss, Walter Benjamin—and everyone who belongs with them—ask me today:
Why did you join the other side in 1933?
So that you would still have a partner on the German side.
A partner in thought, a partner in conversation, and—as my fate from 1945 until today demonstrates—even a partner in fate.
Because without sharing that fate, all this partnership in thought and conversation is worthless.

(Thought and written while preparing a lecture on Hamlet, under the impact of Walter Benjamin’s words “sacrifice for the life of the national community that is not yet born,” The Origin of German Tragic Drama, 1930, p. 99.)
An anticlerical man says to me: Watch out for the priests. Every priest is hungry for power and eager to rule, and possesses ancient tricks for subjecting people to himself.
But why are you telling me this?
I have known it for a long time.
The only thing I notice, listening to you, is that every human being is a priest.
Perhaps that is the effect of the universal priesthood.
Homo homini Clericus. Man is a cleric to man.
Desire conceives and gives birth to sin! So use contraceptives!
Horrible to imagine that—or to picture it.
But perhaps the will to eternity that Nietzsche places inside desire is precisely this conception of sin. Just as it is not power itself but the will to power that is sinful.
Michel Mourre, Lamennais, p. 141: “Féli, you must surrender! You know it perfectly well, Féli. ‘Society’ means, first of all, your failing bookselling business; it means your creditors …” (p. 172).

The cruelty of this method of psychoanalytic-sociological explanation! No human being can survive it. The trick is to seize the initiative with this poisonous weapon of psychological and social analysis—to strike first and paralyze the other person before it even occurs to him to defend himself.
Did I not do exactly the same thing to Adam Müller myself?
Adam Müller was a successful arriviste.
Lamennais was a poor young man driven mad by faith.

And Michel Mourre places himself on the side of authority, which of course is always right—siempre ragione—on the side of the celibate bureaucracy, which of course can never itself become an object of psychoanalysis and whose sociology not even Max Weber dared to write.
Under the impact of the news from Adenauer’s trip to Moscow (9–14 September 1955): The world in which Professor Wilhelm Grewe’s little light shines lies behind me now, an insubstantial semblance.
The full-blooded Moju can do it better; He sharpens the ritual-murder knife.
Am I supposed to long for the satisfaction promised by the thought of posthumous fame?

Am I supposed to look to posterity for comfort—for some vindication like the one Johann Jacob Reiske of the eighteenth century received from Wilamowitz-Moellendorff at the end of the nineteenth century?
